# Project Memory Index Size as a Recurring Per-Session Cost

On 2026-09-30 a `doctor-plus` context audit found the project memory index had grown to roughly 8,200 characters — a cost paid at the start of every session, because the index is auto-loaded rather than retrieved on demand. The index was trimmed from 8,162 to 5,549 characters (~30% smaller) by rewriting each line to state only *when to open* the file it points at, leaving all dates, counts, and error text inside the memory files themselves. All 56 links were verified after the rewrite.

## Key Points

- **The index is always-loaded, so its size is a standing tax**, not a one-time storage cost; growth that would be unremarkable in a retrievable file is expensive here.
- **The durable fix is a line-format rule, not a one-off cut:** each index line states only the condition under which a reader should open the target file. Details belong in the target.
- **Trim measured 8,162 → 5,549 chars (~30%)** with no pointer removed — the reduction came entirely from moving content down a tier, not from dropping entries.
- **All 56 links were verified after the rewrite**, because a reformatting pass over a pointer file is exactly the operation most likely to produce a dangling pointer.
- **This is the same lever applied one layer out** from the Tier A index trim (15 → 10 files) and the repeated `MEMORY.md` cap trims, and it has the same failure mode: without a format rule, the file re-grows.

## Details

A pointer index occupies an unusual position in the memory architecture: it is the mechanism by which content becomes retrievable rather than resident, and yet it is itself resident. That makes it the one file where restating a fact is doubly expensive — the fact is paid for in the index every session *and* stored again in the file the index points at. The observed growth to ~8,200 characters came from exactly that duplication: index lines had accumulated dates, counts, and error strings that already existed in their targets, apparently on the reasoning that a richer index saves a read. The trim rejects that trade, because a read is conditional and cheap while the index is unconditional.

Encoding the fix as a line *format* rather than a size target is what distinguishes this pass from the earlier wording-compression attempts on `MEMORY.md` catalogued in [[concepts/memory-cap-relief-by-migration-not-deletion]]. Compression shortens prose and buys bytes that are immediately re-spent; a format rule ("state when to open this file, nothing else") answers the question that produces the growth in the first place, so the next person adding an entry knows what not to write. It also makes the index auditable: a line containing a date or a count is visibly out of format and can be fixed without a judgment call about whether it is worth its bytes. This is the same move as recording a mechanism instead of a magic number in [[connections/document-the-mechanism-not-the-magic-number]] — the abstraction level of the recorded content is chosen to match how stable that content is.

The link verification step matters because a bulk reformat is precisely the operation that silently breaks pointers. Fifty-six links rewritten by hand or by pattern is fifty-six chances to mistype a target, and a broken index entry is worse than a verbose one: a verbose entry costs tokens, while a dangling one resolves to nothing and makes a real memory file invisible. Verifying after the pass rather than trusting the edit is the same discipline as re-running the doctor to confirm a cap fix, and the same hazard as the stale-pointer class described in [[connections/a-stale-pointer-resolves-cleanly-to-the-wrong-answer]].

# Memory Recall Evaluation Harness (30-Question Retrieval Benchmark)

The recall-eval harness is a scheduled benchmark that scores competing memory-retrieval methods against a fixed 30-question set, writing results to `~/.claude/audits/recall-eval/LATEST.md`. On 2026-10-01 a manual run against a freshly built vault index produced the first fully-scoreable comparison of four methods, and its numbers were used to adjudicate whether the Docker/Milvus-backed memsearch stack should be retired in favor of a cheaper alternative. The harness exists precisely so that a retrieval-infrastructure decision is settled by measurement rather than by cost intuition.

## Key Points

- **Four methods, 30 questions (2026-10-01 run):** memsearch 29/30 hit@5, 15 hit@1, 5.7 s; fts5 + Jev 27/30, 19 hit@1, 0.4 s; plain fts5 25/30, 20 hit@1, 5 ms; `rg` 23/30, 11 hit@1, 111 ms. Coverage was 14/14 Tier A notes and 12/13 vault notes.
- **Pre-registered retirement rule:** memsearch is retired only if a cheaper method comes within 1 hit@5. fts5+Jev trails by 2, so the rule did not fire and the Docker/Milvus stack was kept.
- **Recall and ranking diverge.** memsearch wins hit@5 but loses hit@1 (15 vs plain fts5's 20) — it is better at *finding* the right note than at *ranking* it first. A single headline metric would have hidden this.
- **Indexing the vault changed the verdict's availability, not just its value.** Before the overnight index, memsearch was unscoreable; after it (started 22:30, finished 02:49, 259 minutes, 8,302 chunks) it became the best method on recall.
- **The scheduled run failed silently and is not yet diagnosed.** The eval task queued after the index died within ~7 seconds, runs fine by hand, and Task Scheduler history is disabled on the laptop — so the fix is to add output logging to the task before the next Sunday 02:00 run rather than to guess at a cause.

## Details

The harness's value on 2026-10-01 came less from any single score than from the structure it imposed on a decision. The question on the table — keep a Docker/Milvus semantic-search stack or drop to SQLite FTS5 — is exactly the kind of question that gets answered by vibes: the cheaper method is dramatically faster (5 ms versus 5.7 s) and carries no container dependency, and a stopped Milvus container had already caused days of memsearch timeouts (see [[concepts/memsearch-tool-maintenance]]). A pre-registered bar — "within 1 hit@5" — prevented that convenience from deciding the matter. fts5+Jev landed 2 behind, the rule did not fire, and memsearch stayed. This is the same discipline as writing a pass bar before running a model (see [[concepts/pre-registered-pass-bar]]) and the same demand that a model be justified by the failure of the strongest cheap alternative rather than any alternative (see [[connections/measured-baseline-before-model-adoption]]) — here the cheap alternatives were genuinely strong, and the rule was honored in the direction of keeping the expensive tool.

The hit@5 / hit@1 split is the run's most useful substantive finding. Reporting both metrics exposed a behavioral difference the aggregate obscures: memsearch retrieves the relevant note into the top five almost always (29/30) but places it first only half the time (15/30), while plain FTS5 misses more often (25/30) yet ranks precisely when it hits (20/30). Characterized plainly, memsearch is a recall instrument and lexical search is a precision instrument, which argues for using them for different jobs rather than picking one winner. It also means any future retirement test must keep reporting both numbers, since a method that matched memsearch on hit@5 while beating it on hit@1 would be a strict improvement, whereas one that matched on hit@5 alone would be a lateral move.

Two operational lessons attach to the run. First, the overnight index's 259-minute duration confirms that full-library embedding is an hours-scale job belonging to a scheduled task, consistent with the earlier relocation of the heavy reindex into the nightly backup. Second, the eval task's ~7-second death is currently uninformative: it reproduces only under the scheduler, the obvious candidate causes (encoding, a missing API key) were ruled out, and the scheduler's own history is disabled. The chosen response was not a workaround but an instrumentation change — add output logging so the next scheduled failure captures a real error — because an unlogged scheduled job that works by hand supplies no diagnostic surface at all.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

# 5 Slides in 5 Minutes: Deck Evidence Corrections and Topic Expansion

On 2026-10-06, two Codex sessions worked the `Education_Alignment_Initiative` (EAI) project's 40-deck "5 Slides in 5 Minutes" (5S5M) staff-education library for Baylor Athletics. The first adjudicated a direct contradiction between two decks against the primary acute-exercise literature and corrected four decks; the second proposed five new topics (41–45) to fill thin categories and bring the pipeline to the 45 topics the program documents already describe. Neither session committed, and both left explicit review steps for Eric.

## Key Points

- **Deck 13 was closer to the evidence than Deck 01, and both were corrected.** Deck 01 asserted a post-practice "cognitive deficit"; Deck 13 held that post-exercise thinking is slightly sharper with any drag attributable to dehydration, hunger, or rush. The literature (Chang et al. 2025 *Psychol Bull*; Lambourne & Tomporowski 2010 *Brain Res*) supports improvement on average, including after fatiguing protocols, with no established universal dip or recovery deadline after a ~2-hour hard practice.
- **The surviving limits are conditional, not universal,** and were put on-slide: prolonged exercise in extreme heat reduced visuomotor accuracy even with water replacement (Wittbrodt et al. 2018, *Physiol Rep*), and dehydration impairment is greater above 2% body-mass loss (Wittbrodt & Millard-Stafford 2018, *MSSE*).
- **A chart was silently misrepresenting its source.** Deck 31's slope chart had been drawing one data point twice; it was replaced with plain bars showing 31.7%, 24.6%, 15.5%, 10.1% once each (Fransen et al. 2014), with the `docs/LIBRARY_PLAN.md` row updated to match.
- **Fictional data is permissible only when labeled as such.** Deck 33's generic "Program A–F" placeholders were replaced with named Baylor sports in a calendar explicitly marked fictional — no invented data presented as real.
- **Topics 41–45 target category gaps, not general coverage:** REDs (Nutrition & Fueling), Concussion Reporting Culture (Cross-Functional Integration), Exertional Heat Illness (Recovery & Load Management), Measurement Error: Is the Change Real? (Sport Science & Technology), and Retrieval Practice (Contextual Engineering & Education Delivery).
- **Two mechanical constraints recur in this library:** hero layout IDs must stay unique across all 40 decks (re-verified after the deck 31 change), and department naming must read Athletic Performance / Athletic Medicine / Applied Performance.

## Details

The Deck 01 / Deck 13 adjudication is the most transferable part of the session, because it shows what a contradiction between two of a library's own decks is actually evidence of. Two slides authored at different times made incompatible claims about the same phenomenon, and the resolution was not to average them or to pick the more recent one but to read the primary literature and discover that the *direction* of the commonly repeated claim was wrong: acute exercise improves cognition on average rather than depressing it. The "post-practice cognitive deficit" framing is intuitive, widely assumed in applied settings, and unsupported as a universal effect. What survived was a narrower set of conditional findings — heat and >2% body-mass dehydration — which is a different and more defensible teaching point than a blanket dip. An internal contradiction in a teaching library is therefore better read as a prompt to check both sides against sources than as a formatting inconsistency to reconcile.

The Deck 31 slope chart is the session's sharpest tooling lesson and a close relative of the automated layout-QA limits found in the deck-generator work. The chart rendered without error and looked like a legitimate visualization of a trend while in fact plotting one of its four data points twice — a defect invisible to any structural check because the file was valid and the layout was clean. The honest fallback was the less sophisticated form: four bars, each value once. This is the same trade the newsletter and deck-render work keeps surfacing, where a visual aid that cannot be trusted to represent its input is worse than a plainer one that can. Deck 33's fix runs on the same axis of honesty at a different layer: naming real Baylor sports makes a scheduling example legible, and the only thing that keeps it from becoming fabricated data is the explicit fictional label.

The topic-expansion session is notable for what it deliberately did *not* do. It was read-only apart from one new proposal file (`docs/TOPICS_41-45_PROPOSAL.md`), making no edits to `references/topic-library.md` or any deck, and no commit — leaving the append of entries 41–45 into the five-slides-generator skill's topic library, plus the EAI `docs/STATUS.md` and `decks/manifest.md` updates, as reviewable follow-ups. Topic 44 ("Measurement Error: Is the Change Real?") is self-referentially apt given that Baylor's own force-plate reliability analysis found no CMJ metric resolves the smallest worthwhile change at weekly cadence. Two operational residues carried out of the day: the `.git` directory in `Education_Alignment_Initiative` was read-only, blocking `git pull` and leaving every change uncommitted, and a parallel edit thread on decks 18, 20, and 39 (crisis line) stayed untouched — the same decks that reappeared in the evening closeout as needing referral-path placeholders filled, there numbered 18, 20, 39, 42, 43.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/five-slides-five-minutes-deck-series]] — The deck series and its renderer; this session corrects four of its decks and proposes five new topics.
- [[concepts/automated-layout-qa-gate]] — The gate that passes a chart which is structurally valid but semantically wrong, exactly the Deck 31 failure.
- [[concepts/powerpoint-free-pptx-renderer]] — The `deck.js` / `deck.pptx` / `deck.html` output trio these corrections were regenerated through.
- [[concepts/compression-amplifies-distortion]] — A five-slide format strips the qualifiers that made the heat and dehydration findings conditional, which is how a universal "deficit" claim gets onto a slide.
- [[connections/real-citations-do-not-validate-claims]] — The Matt Jordan CMJ document in the same day's RTP work is the extreme case: real-looking sourcing that traces to Instagram posts.
- [[concepts/forceplate-decisionsystem-metric-reliability]] — The in-house measurement-error finding that proposed topic 44 would teach.
- [[concepts/statistical-inference-audit-checklist]] — The audit patterns that distinguish "improves on average" from "no dip ever" and conditional from universal claims.
- [[concepts/applied-performance-digest-build]] — The parallel Baylor documentation effort sharing the Athletic Performance / Athletic Medicine / Applied Performance naming convention.

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-10-06.md]] — Codex evidence-correction session (09:20): Deck 01 vs Deck 13 contradiction adjudicated against Chang et al. 2025 and Lambourne & Tomporowski 2010, retained heat/dehydration limits (Wittbrodt 2018 ×2), Deck 33 labeled-fictional calendar with named Baylor sports, Deck 31 slope chart drawing one point twice replaced with Fransen et al. 2014 bars, hero layout ID uniqueness re-verified, read-only `.git` blocking `git pull`, nothing committed, `scripts/export.ps1` and `scripts/qa.js` deliberately left to Eric, decks 18/20/39 crisis-line thread untouched. Topic-proposal session (09:38): topics 41–45 chosen to fill thin categories, constraints honored (no deck or `topic-library.md` edits, no commit, department naming preserved), follow-up append and STATUS/manifest updates queued.

===END ARTICLE===

# HPI Return-to-Performance Manual: V3 Gap Audit and Phased Goal Prompt

On 2026-10-06 a three-phase goal prompt was drafted for reviewing and completing the Baylor High Performance Initiative (HPI) Return-to-Performance Manual, and Phase 1 — the gap audit — was executed. Sources live on Google Drive under `01_ACTIVE_PROJECTS/01_ONGOING/HighPerformanceInitative_RTP/`; outputs were saved as `Docs\HPI_RTP_Manual_GoalPrompt.md` and `Docs\HPI_RTP_Manual_V4_GapAudit.md`. The audit found roughly two-thirds of V3 (Apr 15 2026) is still bracketed guidance text, that the document contradicts itself on the most basic structural questions, and that five referenced files do not exist in the folder.

## Key Points

- **Three conflicting stage counts coexist in one manual:** §3.1 says five stages, the rehab templates use six, and the workload model uses four steps. There is no canonical test list either — the intake matrix, the templates, `HPI_DataDepot.xlsx`, and the workflow document each enumerate a different set, and Nordic, IMTP, and FMS are collected in practice but absent from the manual.
- **Pass thresholds are asserted without citation while the manual elsewhere says thresholds are pending.** Templates state ≥80/90% limb symmetry, FMS >14, and DASH ≥90 with zero sources, yet §7.3 still says thresholds await Kitman.
- **Only seven sections plus the LE/UE rehab templates have real content** (3.2, 3.3, 8.3, 8.4, 9.1, 11); the rest is bracketed guidance. Every rollout date has passed — not only the June 1 2026 effective date — and the May 7 Q&A appendix is stale.
- **Five referenced files are missing from the source folder:** the injury classification document, testing record form, clearance sign-off form, NCAA best-practices document, and force-plate metric appendix.
- **V3 is the source of truth and V4 is a new file.** Older outlines are history only, V3's deliberate cuts (intake form, referral forms) stay cut, and V3 is never overwritten. Unresolved items route to `HPI_RTP_Manual_V4_OpenItems.md` with an owner and a proposed default.
- **Sections owned by others are drafted, not invented.** Jeremy (3/4/5/12), JB (10), and Jacob/Josh (glossary) sections are drafted from source documents and tagged "DRAFT FOR <owner> REVIEW", with no invented clinical criteria.
- **A sourcing document was downgraded to a lead-finder.** The Matt Jordan CMJ document is usable only to trace original papers, because some of its own sources are Instagram posts.

## Details

The audit's central finding is that the manual's unresolved items are not evenly distributed — they cluster at the two decisions everything else depends on. D1 (the stage model) and D2 (the canonical test battery) block drafting Sections 3 through 7 outright, which is why they were flagged as mattering most. A document that cannot say how many stages a return-to-performance progression has, or which tests gate movement between them, cannot have its middle written regardless of how much prose is added; the three conflicting counts are not three drafting errors but one unmade decision rendered three times. This is the inverse of the usual documentation-completion problem: the bottleneck is a small number of owner decisions rather than volume of writing.

The citation findings deserve separate emphasis because they cut in two directions. Downward, the templates already assert concrete numeric pass thresholds (≥80/90% limb symmetry, FMS >14, DASH ≥90) with no sources at all, while §7.3 simultaneously claims thresholds are awaiting Kitman — so the document both asserts and disclaims its own gates. Upward, the Matt Jordan CMJ document looked like a sourcing shortcut and was explicitly demoted to a lead-finder on inspection, because a reference whose own citations include Instagram posts transfers no inferential license even where the underlying papers are real. The correct use is to trace through it to primary literature, which is the same discipline applied the same day to the 5S5M deck corrections and the same failure class as treating a verified citation as a validated claim.

The prompt engineering itself produced a reusable pattern. Eric asked twice for the handoff prompt to be tightened, with two specific requirements: it must begin with `/goal`, and it must be paste-ready with no brackets left to fill in. The final version accepts all defaults D1–D8 and marks anything only Eric can answer as `[CONFIRM: Eric]` — so the prompt is runnable immediately by anyone while still surfacing, rather than silently guessing, the facts that require the owner. Phase 2 is designed to stop before the Phase 3 final save and report its `[CONFIRM: Eric]` items. The Eric-only answers still outstanding are a new effective date and hard launch target; what actually happened during the rollout (May 7 presentation, June 1 soft launch, June 3 training, physician briefing); leadership approval status for the performance-meeting framework and physician written clearance; whether the Kitman collaboration remains active; and the locations of the five missing files. Terminology follows Eric's convention throughout (Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance) because the manual goes to administration, and Section 8 names roles rather than individuals.

# Mac Sleep Freezes Long Drive-Reading Scripts

On 2026-10-06 a `landed.py` project-file scan showed no progress because it was frozen rather than slow: the Mac slept at 09:09, three minutes into the run, and the scan remained frozen on a Google Drive folder even after the machine woke. Re-running it with the Mac held awake via `caffeinate` completed in about four minutes. The fix generalizes an existing pattern — the backup skill had already been placed under `caffeinate` the same day — into a rule for any long Drive-reading script on the Mac.

## Key Points

- **A frozen run and a slow run look identical from the outside.** The question "how are you doing on this?" returned nothing not because the scan was mid-progress but because it had stopped; the absence of output was the whole signal available.
- **Waking the Mac does not resume the scan.** The freeze survived wake, so sleep during a Drive read is not a pause but a permanent stall requiring a re-run — meaning there is no "wait longer" recovery.
- **The true runtime was about four minutes.** Under `caffeinate` the same scan finished quickly, which retroactively proves the original hang was environmental rather than a performance problem in the script.
- **Sleep prevention belongs on the script, not on the operator.** The durable remedy is wrapping long Drive-reading work in `caffeinate` — the same change already applied to the backup skill — rather than remembering to keep the machine awake.
- **The scan's scope was also wrong:** `landed.py` reads `05_SYSTEMS/AI_Sessions_Backup`, a large session-backup folder that likely should be excluded, so part of the duration was work it should not have been doing.

## Details

The diagnostic shape here is worth separating from the fix. A long-running job that emits nothing is ambiguous between "working" and "dead", and the ambiguity is resolved only by changing a condition and re-running — here, holding the machine awake. That the second run took four minutes is what converts the first run's silence from "this is an expensive scan" into "this stalled at minute three", because a four-minute baseline makes an indefinite hang unmistakable. Without that comparison the natural response would have been to wait, or to tune the script, both of which would have left the real cause (a host power-state transition during a network-backed filesystem read) untouched. The failure also has the signature of a killed-or-suspended operation that does not self-heal: the resource it was reading became unavailable mid-read, and the process neither errored nor recovered when conditions returned.

The two remedies operate at different layers and both are needed. Sleep prevention addresses the environment the script runs in, and placing it inside the script rather than in the operator's habits is what makes it durable — the backup skill had already taken this form, so the correction is really the recognition that `landed.py` belongs to the same class of work and should have inherited the same treatment. Excluding `05_SYSTEMS/AI_Sessions_Backup` addresses the work set: a project-file scan that sweeps a large session-backup folder is spending its runtime on material that is not a project file, which both lengthens the exposure window to a sleep event and measures the wrong thing. Both items were explicitly deferred to a later project-triage day rather than fixed during the closeout, consistent with the rule that closeout reports drift instead of repairing it.

- [[connections/the-execution-context-silently-edits-the-work-set]] — A host-state change shrinking or stopping what a run attempts without producing an error.

# Mac Stack Cleanup Closeout (2026-10-06)

The 2026-10-06 Mac `/closeout` run followed a day of Claude-stack cleanup and is notable chiefly for what it declined to do: it left the nightly backup configuration unchanged (Option A), wrote no `STATUS.md` updates because no project repository had real work that day, and left 14 items of registry drift unfixed on the standing rule that closeout reports drift but never repairs it. Five repositories were pushed, and the handoff was written to `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/2026-10-06-mac-stack-cleanup.md`.

## Key Points

- **Closeout reports drift, it does not fix it.** Fourteen registry-drift items were surfaced and deliberately left alone; repair belongs to a project-triage pass, not to the end-of-day sweep.
- **No `STATUS.md` writes is a legitimate closeout outcome.** With no project repo carrying real work, writing status entries would have manufactured activity records — the same judgment as recording a compile that produced nothing as a complete result.
- **Five repositories pushed, each with a distinct payload:** dotclaude (skill override settings, memory note, session files), claude-skills (stack-check fix, backup skill wrapped in `caffeinate`), global-memory (shortened `USER.md` and `MEMORY.md`, handoff, file ledger), and graphify-out (two nightly snapshots).
- **The skill-override change needs a restart to verify.** The carried action is to restart Claude Code, type `/`, and confirm `watch` and `last30days` each appear exactly once — an activation step that does not travel with the committed settings.
- **A still-running nightly job makes `graphify-out` deliberately unfinished.** More changes may land there, with the next morning's `/startup` designated to push them rather than holding the closeout open.

## Details

The session's governing discipline is scope separation between reporting and repairing. Registry drift, the duplicate-skill question, and the `landed.py` resilience work were all identified and all routed forward — to project triage, to a post-restart check, and to another day respectively — rather than absorbed into the closeout. The payoff is that a closeout run has a bounded, predictable cost and cannot silently turn into an open-ended maintenance session; the cost is that drift items recur across days and accumulate a visible age, which the triage-digest work has separately shown is the characteristic weakness of a visibility-optimizing process. The Option A decision on the nightly backup configuration is the same restraint applied to a configuration question: the explicit choice to leave it as it is, recorded as a decision, is more useful than an unexamined non-change.

The verification residue is the part most likely to matter later. Two of the day's changes cannot be confirmed from within the session that made them: the skill-override settings require a Claude Code restart before `/` will show whether `watch` and `last30days` are each listed once, and the `graphify-out` snapshots depend on a nightly job that is still running. Both were handled by naming the confirming action and its expected observation rather than by asserting success — restart and count the entries; let `/startup` push whatever arrived. This is the same pattern as handing a verification over as one command with a pre-stated expected output, and it is what keeps a closeout's claims honest when the owning layer is a process the session cannot query. The per-machine nature of the restart requirement is itself the familiar hazard: committed settings propagate, but the loaded state that makes them take effect does not.

# Performance_Playbook Open Questions Answered In-Session

At the 2026-10-06 closeout for the annual-report delivery day, three of the Performance_Playbook (Applied Performance Digest) open questions carried from 2026-10-04 were answered and marked ANSWERED in `docs/STATUS.md`. The receiver was recorded as Applied Performance (primary) with the Health and Wellness department at large as secondary, closing the portfolio card's "needs a receiver" gap; chapter 1's daily users and co-owners were set as Applied Performance and Athletic Performance staff; and the chapter was decided *not* to retire the Operations Guide's ForceDecks section when it ships on 10/23.

## Key Points

- **The receiver answer was written in two places:** `portfolio.json` and `Performance_Playbook/docs/STATUS.md`, which is what closed the portfolio card's "needs a receiver" gap rather than merely answering the question in conversation.
- **Naming the daily users also fixed the review date's subject.** Applied Performance and Athletic Performance staff are simultaneously the 10/23 ship target and the audience for the 11/22 30-day check, so the chapter acquires an owner and a review constituency in one decision.
- **The chapter does not replace the Operations Guide's ForceDecks section.** Both stay in use until the AP Digest covers the whole operations manual — a coexistence decision rather than a migration.
- **Coexistence creates a mirroring obligation, recorded as a gotcha.** Two live documents covering the same material means a change to one must be mirrored in the other, which was noted in Performance_Playbook's STATUS.
- **Answering STATUS `## Open questions` in-session and marking them ANSWERED is what keeps them off the next morning's `/startup` decisions list** — the extraction mechanism reads the file, so the resolution has to land in the file.

## Details

The receiver and daily-user answers are the same kind of move as naming a review date: each converts a document into something with a named constituency. A digest chapter with no recorded receiver is an artifact; one addressed to Applied Performance with Health and Wellness as a secondary audience is a deliverable that can be judged against whether those people use it. Writing the answer into both `portfolio.json` and the project's own STATUS is what makes the closure visible to two different readers — a portfolio review scanning cards for gaps, and a session opening the project directly — and it is the same dual-write discipline applied elsewhere when a decision has more than one natural lookup path.

The ForceDecks decision is the most consequential of the three because it was a genuine fork. Chapter 1 could have been declared the replacement for the Operations Guide's ForceDecks section on ship, retiring the older text and leaving one authoritative source; instead both were kept live until the Digest covers the full operations manual. That is defensible — a partial replacement would leave the operations manual with a hole — but it knowingly accepts a two-source condition for the same material, and the session recorded the resulting obligation explicitly as a STATUS gotcha: a change to either document has to be mirrored in the other. Recording the cost at the moment of the decision is what distinguishes an accepted trade-off from latent drift, since the same paired-document condition has already produced a real access-rule divergence in the NCAA best-practices guide and its athlete-facing appendix.

The procedural lesson is narrower and mechanical. STATUS `## Open questions` entries feed the next morning's `/startup` decisions list through an extractor that reads the file, so a question answered in conversation but left unmarked keeps reappearing, while a question marked ANSWERED in place disappears from the morning surface. This is the same constraint that earlier required open questions to be stated inline rather than pointed at another document — the consumer cannot dereference, and it cannot read the session transcript either.

# Connection: A Chart Can Be Valid, Clean, and Still Lying About Its Source

## The Connection

Deck 31's slope chart rendered without error, passed whatever structural checks the deck pipeline applies, and plotted one of its four data points twice. Nothing in the file was malformed; the defect lived entirely in the relationship between the rendered mark and the Fransen et al. 2014 figures it claimed to show. The same day's RTP gap audit found the mirror-image defect in prose: templates asserting ≥80/90% limb symmetry, FMS >14, and DASH ≥90 — numbers that are syntactically perfect, internally consistent with each other, and attached to no source at all.

## Key Insight

The checks that exist in these pipelines all operate on the artifact's internal properties, and source fidelity is not an internal property. A layout gate can verify that nothing collides and that hero layout IDs are unique across forty decks; it cannot verify that four bars correspond to four distinct numbers in a paper. A document build can confirm every section renders; it cannot confirm that a threshold has a citation. This means the entire class of "does this artifact represent its input honestly?" defects is invisible to automated validation by construction — and such defects are *more* dangerous than malformed output, because malformed output announces itself while a clean chart actively recruits trust.

The corollary is that the honest fallback is often the less sophisticated form. Deck 31's fix was plain bars showing each of 31.7%, 24.6%, 15.5%, 10.1% once; the slope chart's extra expressiveness had bought a trend narrative that the data did not contain. A visual aid whose correctness cannot be checked is worth less than a plainer one whose correctness is obvious on inspection — the same reasoning that led the kickoff-GIF rework to fix the viewport rather than ask the human to look harder, and that led the deck layout gate's authors to record explicitly that it cannot see text overflowing its own box.

## Evidence

- **Deck 31 (2026-10-06):** a slope chart drawing one data point twice, replaced with four plain bars from Fransen et al. 2014, with the `docs/LIBRARY_PLAN.md` row updated to match. The defect was caught by reading the chart against the source, not by any gate.
- **Hero layout IDs:** re-verified for uniqueness across all 40 decks after the change — an example of exactly the internal property automation *can* check, run in the same session as the defect it could not.
- **RTP templates (2026-10-06):** ≥80/90% limb symmetry, FMS >14, DASH ≥90 asserted with zero citations, while §7.3 of the same manual says thresholds await Kitman — the artifact simultaneously asserting and disclaiming its own gates.
- **Matt Jordan CMJ document:** demoted to a lead-finder for tracing original papers because some of its own sources are Instagram posts — real-looking provenance that transfers no inferential license.
- **Deck 33:** named Baylor sports in a calendar kept legitimate only by an explicit fictional label, showing that the fix for unverifiable content can be disclosure rather than removal.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_scrape
entries.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. A named browser profile loads saved session data without saving changes to it.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

profile.description: Loads a saved browser profile without saving changes to it.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search
entries.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, `developer`, or `gov`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

For a legal or regulatory question, `categories: ["gov"]` returns results in `data.web` with `category: "gov"` and cannot be combined with other categories; `firecrawl_gov_search` is the dedicated tool. Verify gov results' issuer, jurisdiction, status, and version before citing current law.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

objective.description: Optional broader goal for this search, if known. Avoid sensitive information.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation; `gov` searches the Government Index of US federal, state, and local legal and regulatory sources, the index behind firecrawl_gov_search, and cannot be combined with other categories; gov hits can include historical versions, bill text, agency guidance, and third-party reproductions, so verify the issuer, jurisdiction, enacted/effective status, and version before citing current governing law, clarify a missing jurisdiction or ambiguous as-of date, and use general search for non-US questions or missing coverage (no hits does not establish that no applicable law exists). `developer` and `gov` return hits in `data.web` with `category` set to their name; the other categories also filter `data.web`.
